item.title: Trends in Psychological First Aid After Disasters
item.description:
Disaster Psychology

Trends in Psychological First Aid After Disasters

Two scientific reviews examine trends and challenges in psychological first aid.

Posted August 1, 2026

Psychological first aid and mental health first aid can assist anyone experiencing difficulties, including post-disaster populations. Its effectiveness has been demonstrated around the world, such as in Bangladesh, with plenty of opportunities for continuing and improving this work. Two recent scientific reviews offer summaries of and directions for psychological first aid in disasters.

Social work practice

Source: Ilan Kelman

The journal Social Work in Mental Health published a five-author collaboration among researchers in Thailand, Sweden, and Bangladesh. The authors sought and analysed publications on psychological first aid in disasters for social work.

Their search to find these publications used a single academic database and a highly focused set of keywords. For instance, they used “Psychological First Aid” and “PFA,” but do not mention “Mental Health First Aid” and “MHFA.” These categories have overlaps as well as differences. The search’s time frame started in 2000, with the justification that modern psychological first aid emerged around then, and ran to 2025.

The authors imposed no language restrictions, but keywords are listed only in English. The search resulted in 276 publications for analysis.

Their analysis identifies spikes in publication numbers after three major disasters: Haiti’s 2010 earthquake disaster, Japan’s 2011 earthquake and tsunami disaster, and the COVID-19 pandemic, which ran from 2020 to 2023. No explanation is offered for why many other major disasters did not lead to similar increases in publication numbers.

Other analyses included geographic origin of papers, author collaborations, and thematic analyses. No detailed comment is made about how the number of scientists, the number of journals, and the number of papers have expanded substantially over the study period. It is possible that the number of publications on psychological first aid in disasters for social work has increased, but its share of science has decreased due to the rapid expansion of scientific publications.

The paper’s framing differentiated natural disasters from human-made disasters (using the non-gender-neutral term “man-made”), even though baseline disaster research has spent over 50 years explaining why the phrase “natural disaster” is a misnomer and should not be used. The paper also differentiates countries according to income levels without explaining why healthcare, especially mental healthcare, is not necessarily better in certain groups of countries. As a poor person, try getting preventive mental healthcare in the U.S., or consider the length of waiting lists in the U.K. for any form of mental health support.

Trends and developments

The other review was a sole-authored paper from a scientist based in Türkiye, published in the journal Current Psychology and covering a different publications database without time restrictions. The earliest article found was from 1998, and the search was conducted in 2024. As with the first paper, “mental health first aid” and “MHFA” were not listed for the search.

article continues after advertisement

One hundred sixty-eight articles met the criteria, again without language restriction, yet searching in English only according to the reported method. Nonetheless, the author found and included papers in English, Spanish, German, Italian, French, and Portuguese.

A quantitative analysis mapped and interpreted the publications’ content. The author examined author networks, citations, countries, institutions, and keywords. Four clusters of topics appeared: psychological first aid training, disaster mental health and psychosocial support, children, and the COVID-19 pandemic.

The analysis considered the number of publications, explaining why more papers were published after specific disasters, notably the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami disaster; Hurricane Katrina in the U.S. in 2005, which is misreported as being in 2008; the 2011 Japan earthquake and tsunami disaster; and the 2014 to 2016 Ebola outbreak, referred to as both a “pandemic” and an “epidemic.” COVID-19 features prominently, and a major increase in publication numbers is attributed to this outbreak. The author notes that the two journals publishing the most papers on psychological first aid in disasters are the two journals publishing the most papers overall among the journals publishing in this field.

Similarly to the first paper, the paper uses the phrase “natural disaster” uncritically while referring to the common myth of “the increasing frequency and severity of disasters.”

Acting on the analyses

Both papers provide solid recommendations for moving forward with psychological first aid in disasters. Prominent is training and education, especially collaboration among educators, practitioners, and researchers. Contextualising and localising this work is deemed important, supporting people locally to help themselves in disaster response.

The papers mention the importance of including everyone as well as making the best use of digital health, telehealth, and other technological approaches. Plenty of work exists explaining how digitisation increases inclusivity for many and decreases it for many others. The papers’ suggestions for regulations, monitoring, and evaluation apply to ensuring that shifts and advances in how psychological first aid is administered would not leave out anyone.

Despite major efforts and successes in avoiding disasters, calamity continues to devastate lives and societies. Psychological first aid not only helps people get through the worst time of their lives, but also inspires those affected to do better by preventing disasters from happening in the first place.

item.title: 5 Resilience Hacks to Leap Over Life's Roadblocks
item.description:
Mindfulness

5 Resilience Hacks to Leap Over Life's Roadblocks

If you've given up on a goal, you might want to use a mindfulness hack.

Posted August 1, 2026

Key points
  • Most people give up on their New Year goals.
  • Mindfulness helps build resilience and overcome mental obstacles.
  • Present-moment awareness through mindfulness reduces communication problems.
Source: Edu-Lauton / Unsplash

If you have been derailed from reaching a goal, you're not alone. Research has shown, for example, that most people fail to reach their New Year goals. People give up on their goals for many reasons, such as lack of willpower or having vague goals.

One key reason I don't see in the conversation: A lack of mindfulness can cause dis-traction, loss of focus, and a focus on the negative.

The good news? It's well known in psychology that mindfulness is a factor of resilience that supports goal achievement.

The fields of psychology and business administration have identified five ways that mindfulness can play a positive role in any work-related environment—and assist in getting past emotional and other roadblocks:

1. Mindfulness helps you see the bigger picture

Mindfulness focuses on examining things from a broader and more neutral perspective. This can help anyone view the messiness of life and work with acceptance and humor. Ironically, when we release the need to micromanage and constantly be in control, we can more easily see and respond to the bigger picture of what is really happening.

2. Mindfulness sharpens creativity and overcomes the fixed mindset

One of the hallmarks of mindlessness—and the inability to problem-solve obstacles—is being stuck in a fixed mindset, which means you are unable to adapt and be creative. Fixed mindsets are pre-determined cognitive beliefs. One example of an unwillingness to see things differently is typified by the worn phrase, “We’ve always done things this way.” Fixed mindsets can cause conflict, fatigue, and burnout. Another form of fixed mindset is a belief in limits—a creativity killer that produces conformity and stifles innovation, flexibility, and productivity.

A belief in limits can make it hard to find novel ways around obstacles. Overcoming any obstacle requires responsive flexibility and creativity, which mindfulness encourages.

3. Mindfulness widens external attention

The term used for mindfulness, as applied to dynamic task environments where decisions occur rapidly and are interconnected, is a ‘wide external breadth of attention.’ When faced with a roadblock, a wide external attention form of mindfulness helps managers (and others) to improvise in the face of unexpected challenges, and to make interdependent decisions in real time, which is to say, “fight fires” and respond to crises.

Successful improvisation in both reaching goals and in business depends on being attentive and alert to what is happening in the here and now.

4. Mindfulness increases awareness of negative self-talk

Mindfulness is an effective means of noticing and interrupting irrational and negative self-talk. Awareness of your inner negative dialogue helps maintain positivity and optimism, rather than focusing on obstacles or failures that are best understood as part of the learning process.

5. Mindfulness addresses communication problems

At its core, mindfulness helps anyone maintain present-moment awareness openly, without defensiveness and judgment. This is essential for communicating and listening to others, as well as minimizing miscommunication.

Conclusion

These five elements are essential ingredients for resilience and reaching goals. Simply Mindful Resilience features 101 daily tools for building resilience that will change your mindset and your experience of obstacles. These mindfulness tools shift one's focus away from what's not working; a gentle attitude of acceptance, positivity, and optimism toward goals may be more effective.

Should you risk setting new goals? By all means, yes! Just be sure to bring a supportive and healthy dose of mindfulness and resilience along for the ride.

item.title: How to Rediscover Meaning in Life After Loss
item.description:
Grief

How to Rediscover Meaning in Life After Loss

A sense of coherence can shape depression and satisfaction after loss.

Posted August 1, 2026

Key points
  • Meaning may enhance healthy responses to loss and reduce unhealthy ones.
  • Experiencing growth through loss can decrease loneliness.
  • Support from others and steady meaning-making are vital in moving forward.

The burden of loss affects each of us at one time or another. Yet each experience involves a unique behavioral and emotional response. Research has explored the broad range of responses to grief and loss, which may help people in grief to move forward.

The Comfort of Coherence

Paul A. Boelen and Maja O’Connor (2022) examined the value of having a sense of coherence during a period of prolonged grief, depression, and life satisfaction after bereavement.[i] Examining psychological factors associated with maintaining healthy functioning after suffering an adverse event, they examined the role of a sense of coherence in recovering from loss. They defined this coherence as an orientation to life that includes manageability, comprehensibility, and meaningfulness.

Studying a Danish sample of 221 elderly people who had lost a spouse, Boelen and O’Connor compared sense of coherence factors with symptom levels of prolonged grief disorder and depression, as well as life satisfaction. They assessed these levels after loss at 6, 13, and 18 months. They found the three coherence factors were linked with prolonged grief, depression, and satisfaction with life. Of the three factors, however, they found that meaningfulness (but not manageability and comprehensibility) may enhance healthy responses to loss and reduce unhealthy ones. They acknowledge that assisting bereaved individuals as they navigate daily life is a valuable and necessary component of comprehensive grief support.

Post Loss Recovery: Making Meaning and Personal Growth

Catherine H. Stein and colleagues examined the process of meaning-making after loss in a younger population.[ii] In a study of 111 young adults responding to personal loss, they examined the use of religious, benefit finding, and goal-oriented meaning-making strategies. The types of loss most commonly reported by their participants were relationship loss and death of a loved one.

Stein and colleagues note that their study conceptualizes stress-related personal growth as a process of meaning-making rather than a result of reappraising the situation. Their results suggest that young people experience and are affected by personal loss, which can influence their strivings, and use religious and benefit-finding strategies to derive meaning from the loss. They also found that the strategies used to create meaning from loss are differentially related to experiencing psychological distress.

Stein and colleagues also note that perceptions about how loss impacts strivings contributed to experiencing loneliness and depressed mood. Young adults who reported that loss discouraged their strivings experienced higher levels of depression, and those who did not perceive loss as impacting their strivings had lower levels of depression. Young adults who reported that loss discouraged their strivings also reported more loneliness. Stein and colleagues report that their findings suggest that for young adults, perceiving loss in a manner that questions future goal orientation or life trajectory creates greater distress, while meaning-making strategies that protect the link between loss and future goals produce less distress.

article continues after advertisement

Regarding loneliness, Stein and colleagues state that generally, young adults who experience higher personal growth through loss also experience less loneliness. Recognizing the link between loneliness, self-presentation, and perceptions of evaluations of others, they suggest that perceptions of personal growth may be linked with positive self-attributions in relationships with others as a result of loss, and reduced perceptions of interpersonal loneliness.

Moving Forward From Loss: Making Meaning, Step by Step

Regardless of age, progress after a personal loss requires finding meaning in the experience, which fosters the motivation and desire to pursue future goals. Focused on a slow and steady path forward, supportive friends and family can assist with individual resilience and recovery. In addition, and professional help is available.
